speaker: Ryan Petersen
title: Ryan Petersen: Building Flexport into a B Logistics Giant
question: In global freight logistics, how does owning your own planes or ships change your incentives toward customers?
guest: It really helped us during those few years of COVID when there was tight capacity—we could serve people when no one else could. But it was a real education about asset ownership in logistics, in that it kind of turns you against your customers in some ways that can be unhealthy. Because your job when you have a plane or a ship is to fill the plane or the ship. It's not to serve the customer anymore. If the customer's cargo needs to go to a different airport, you'll try to convince them to fly it where your plane is going and then truck it a long distance. Or you say, 'Oh, just wait three days, the plane's leaving in three days,' instead of saying, 'Hey, let me find you a different option.' If you're an asset owner, it's pretty hard to be customer-centric because your job is to fill the asset or you don't make money.

points.core: Owning transport assets shifts priority from serving customers to filling your own capacity.
points.note: Accept: asset utilization pressure, high fixed costs forcing carriers to fill planes/ships/vessels to make money, or structural conflict between asset-heavy ownership and neutral customer service. Do not credit: generic claims that owning assets is expensive or capital-intensive without linking it to misaligned customer incentives.

points.core: Asset owners steer shipments onto their own network instead of optimal external carriers.
points.note: Accept: pushing shippers to fly into the carrier's hub airport plus long-distance trucking, making cargo wait days for the carrier's next departure, or avoiding faster/better third-party options. Do not credit: vague statements that carriers are 'less flexible' without explaining how routing or scheduling gets distorted.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Owning the assets shifts your priority from finding the best routing for the customer to filling your own capacity.

A plane or ship is a huge fixed cost that is incurred whether it sails full or empty, so an asset owner (a carrier like Maersk, or an integrator like FedEx or UPS) is under constant pressure to maximise utilisation and yield. That creates a bias toward steering cargo onto its own network, even when a competitor's route, schedule or price would suit the shipper better. In tight markets, owners are tempted to ration space to the highest-paying cargo; in weak markets, they discount heavily just to cover fixed costs.

An asset-light forwarder (Kuehne+Nagel, Expeditors, Flexport) earns a margin on arranging transport, so it can be carrier-neutral and shop across operators. Its incentives are not pure either: it profits from the spread between what it charges you and what it pays carriers, and it may favour carriers that give it the best buy rates.

The trade-off is control. Owners can guarantee capacity and reliability when space is scarce, while forwarders offer flexibility and choice but can leave you stranded when carriers prioritise their own direct customers.

Owning ships or planes shifts a logistics provider from a neutral broker optimizing for each shipper’s needs to a capital-intensive operator driven by asset utilization. Because vessels and aircraft carry massive fixed costs—financing, crew, maintenance, and scheduled departures—empty space is perishable inventory lost the moment a ship sails or a plane takes off. Consequently, asset owners are heavily incentivized to steer customers onto their own networks, hubs, and timetables to keep load factors high, even when a competitor’s service would be faster, cheaper, or more direct.

This cost structure also reshapes pricing and service across market cycles. In downturns, asset owners often slash rates toward marginal cost just to keep fleets full; during capacity crunches, they wield strong pricing power, prioritizing high-yield spot cargo or major contract shippers while rolling lower-margin freight to later departures. Ultimately, customers lose unbiased routing flexibility because the provider must feed its own fleet first, yet they gain something asset-light forwarders cannot truly promise when global supply chains tighten: direct operational control and guaranteed physical capacity.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Owning planes or ships ("asset-based" carriers like Maersk or FedEx) turns your main job into filling your own capacity. You carry large fixed costs, including depreciation, crews, leases and debt, whether the hold is full or empty. That pushes you to steer cargo onto your own routes and schedules even when a competitor's option would be faster, cheaper or more direct for the shipper. It also pushes you to discount hard in soft markets to cover fixed costs, to put out cargo-volume commitments and loyalty contracts that lock customers in, and to bundle services so the customer stays in your network.

Asset-light forwarders and brokers such as Kuehne+Nagel, DSV or Flexport buy capacity from many carriers. They earn a margin on the shipment rather than on asset use, so they're mostly free to pick whatever mode or carrier suits the customer best. They have their own conflicts, though, such as margin markups and how rates are presented.

The trade-off is that owners give more control and more reliable capacity when markets are tight, like the 2021 shortages. Asset-light players give more neutrality and flexibility, but they're exposed when capacity runs short.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Owning planes or ships shifts a logistics provider's core incentive from finding the best external option for a customer to maximizing the utilization of its own expensive fixed assets. Because aircraft and vessels incur heavy fixed costs whether they move full or empty, asset owners are strongly driven to steer cargo onto their own routes, schedules, and equipment—even when a rival carrier offers a faster transit, a more direct lane, or a lower spot rate. In contrast, asset-light freight forwarders remain carrier-neutral and compete by shopping across the market.

Asset ownership also reshapes how providers treat different customers. To guarantee steady baseline volume and fill empty backhauls, owners favor large, predictable shippers with long-term contracts, while smaller or sporadic shippers face lower priority when capacity tightens. Owners also enforce stricter cutoffs, detention fees, and allocation rules to keep assets turning. At the same time, ownership gives carriers a stronger stake in schedule reliability and guaranteed capacity during disruptions, since they control the fleet directly.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol

Owning planes or ships gives a freight company a strong incentive to keep them full. The company bears much of the cost of a scheduled flight or sailing even if it departs with empty space, so it may offer discounts to fill spare capacity or steer customers toward its own routes and schedules when another carrier would be faster or cheaper.

Ownership also gives the company more control over schedules, capacity, and how it responds to disruptions. That can make service more reliable, especially for customers who need guaranteed space. A freight forwarder that buys capacity from multiple carriers generally has more flexibility to choose the best fit for each shipment, though its rates, margins, and volume commitments can also influence what it recommends.

Owning planes or ships gives you a financial reason to steer customers’ freight onto your own departures. Many costs are fixed, and once a flight or sailing leaves, you lose the chance to sell its empty space. You may therefore offer a customer a good rate to fill that space, but you also have an incentive to favor your own service even when another carrier offers a faster route or a better schedule.

Ownership can benefit customers, too. Controlling capacity makes it easier to reserve space for them when demand is high. A freight forwarder that buys space from multiple carriers generally has more freedom to choose the best fit for each shipment, though advance commitments to buy space can give it a similar incentive to fill particular departures.
